To diagnose failures, we analyze instances where the Vanilla baseline achieves zero accuracy on LExMem, as shown in Figure 3(b).
We compare the accuracy across six capabilities in Figure 3(c).

abstract: Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these exploration tasks, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose LExMem, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate Memory in Long-term Exploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose LExGraph, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LExMem poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas LExGraph achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/LExMem.

sections.body: The introduction argues that existing long-term memory benchmarks test recall of personal facts and task details, but not iterative trial-and-error exploration. The authors model exploration as directed graphs and build LExMem in three stages: graph construction with an evolutionary mechanism, instantiation with scientific research and software design tasks, and QA extraction from structural subgraphs. LExMem contains 224 dialogues and 2,018 QA instances across three graph-derived question types. The paper also proposes LExGraph, which builds a memory graph incrementally from raw dialogues and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing memory benchmarks test recall of facts, so the paper builds LExMem for iterative exploration and LExGraph for memory.

sections.body: Each exploration graph has nine node types and nine relation types. Graph evolution applies predefined mutation rules to an initial graph, and 150 evolved graphs are retained after verification and curation. Seed tasks cover research exploration (100) and software design (50). Graph instantiation pairs each seed task with four distinct evolved graphs, giving 600 candidates; a global consistency check filters 55.8% of them, leaving 259 instantiated graphs. Dialogue expansion yields 224 dialogues averaging 88K tokens. The final QA set has 2,018 instances: 561 dense, 759 sparse, and 698 same-type.
sections.heading: Benchmark Curation
sections.headline: Graph-guided synthesis turns evolved graphs into 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances across three question types.

sections.body: LExGraph splits dialogue into topic-coherent segments using user turns, then stores each segment as a key-value memory node. The key holds a summary and salient facts; the value holds the raw turns. Hierarchical edges attach each new node to the right frontier of the existing tree, following a discourse constraint. Cross-branch edges connect the new node to earlier nodes outside the frontier whose key embeddings exceed a similarity threshold. At query time, nodes are scored by semantic similarity and BM25 and fused by reciprocal rank fusion. A primary set is selected, then neighbor nodes connected to it are added, both under token budgets.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: LExGraph links dialogue segments into memory nodes with hierarchical and cross-branch edges, then retrieves by hybrid scoring.

sections.body: The baselines are ComoRAG, GraphRAG, HippoRAG, HippoRAG2 and LightRAG for retrieval, and LightMem, Mem0 and StructMem for memory. Each baseline builds its own index or memory over the dialogue and then answers with the same backbone LLM. LExMem is scored with token-level F1 and with accuracy (ACC), where a judge gives 1.0, 0.5 or 0.0. For generalization, ACC is reported on the 128K-token subset of BEAM. Backbones are Qwen-3.8 27B and GPT-6 Luna, with gte-Qwen2-1.5B as the embedding model and GPT-4o mini as the ACC judge.
sections.heading: Experimental Setting
sections.headline: LExGraph is compared with five retrieval-based and three memory-based baselines using token overlap and a judge-scored accuracy metric.

sections.body: LExGraph is top overall across backbones and outperforms GraphRAG and LightMem. Retrieval and memory systems all beat the Vanilla baseline. Accuracy on the Same-Type subset drops for most methods; LightMem reaches 68.52 on Dense and 66.61 on Sparse but 56.34 on Same-Type on GPT-6 Luna. LExGraph keeps a solid advantage across all subsets. Error analysis shows Vanilla's failures concentrate in Same-Type questions. Accuracy declines for all methods as evidence nodes increase. On BEAM, LExGraph is top on seven of ten abilities, with an overall score of 0.472. A case study shows LExGraph relating a key finding to two competing hypotheses, which the baselines do not.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: LExGraph achieves the highest overall LExMem performance across backbones and keeps an advantage on all question subsets.

sections.body: Early long-term memory benchmarks evaluate retention of personal facts in open-domain conversation. Later work adds temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, preferences, cognitive memory, multimodal context, hallucination and long-context retrieval. Task-oriented benchmarks track instructions and project state as they update. Memory frameworks store dialogue as summaries, reflections, compressed memories, trees, graphs or hypergraphs. RAG systems build summary trees or entity knowledge graphs. The authors state that these systems mainly capture semantic or entity-level associations, not dialogue progression in which exploration branches, revisits attempts and builds on outcomes.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior memory benchmarks and frameworks target fact recall or semantic and entity links, not the progression of exploration.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the two contributions. LExMem models exploration as evolved graphs and yields 224 dialogues and 2,018 QA instances. LExGraph structures dialogues into memory graphs and gathers evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. The experiments show that existing retrieval and memory frameworks struggle on LExMem. LExGraph shows consistent gains over strong baselines and transfers to external benchmarks. The authors present the benchmark and framework as tools for more reliable conversational agents in long-term exploration.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Existing frameworks struggle on LExMem, while LExGraph improves on strong baselines and transfers to an external long-term memory benchmark.

sections.body: The first limitation is that real exploration dialogues are hard to collect at scale, so LExMem uses synthetic dialogues from instantiated graphs. These allow control over complexity and give ground-truth structure, with quality checked by LLM checks and human evaluation, but may not capture the stylistic diversity of real conversations. The second limitation is that LExMem evaluates memory through question answering rather than whether better memory leads to better exploration decisions. The authors note that open-ended exploration rarely has a unique correct next step and that verifying one would require running experiments, which they leave to future work.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Stated limits are synthetic dialogues and question answering that does not test whether memory improves downstream exploration decisions.

sections.body: The appendix defines nine node types and nine relation types and gives five categories of mutation rules. It describes the 150 seed tasks and how evidence turns are annotated, with an average of 4.12 per instance. Human evaluation of 75 items per level gives averages such as 4.60 for dialogue faithfulness and 4.83 for QA answerability. Baseline settings include a 10-turn window per passage and top-k retrieval. Evidence retrieval results show LExGraph with the highest NDCG at all cutoffs, and at K=20 it gets 0.354 against 0.323 for HippoRAG2 while HippoRAG2 has higher recall, 0.591 against 0.550. Six capability definitions are also given.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists mutation rules, seed task details, evidence annotation, human evaluation, baseline settings, evidence retrieval results and capability definitions.
